title: Delhi Terrace With 500 Native Plants Now Draws 100 Bird Species
excerpt: Conservationist Aman Sharma turned a bare rooftop into an urban ecosystem during the 2020 lockdown — and shared a three-plant formula anyone can copy, starting with a single host plant.
body:
• Aman Sharma, 23, turned his family's bare Delhi terrace into a rooftop ecosystem of more than 500 native plants during the Covid-19 lockdown.
  • The terrace has documented more than 100 bird species and 25 butterfly species; earlier this year, The Better India reported the bird count had crossed 200 as the habitat matured.
  • His formula for anyone: plant three types — host plants (lemon) for butterfly breeding, flowering plants (sadabahar, bougainvillea) for pollinators, and food-bearing plants (chikoo, guava, pomegranate, capsicum, brinjal) for birds. Start with a single host plant on a balcony or window; add the other two as the space grows.
  • A Los Angeles filmmaker who saw The Better India's coverage invited Sharma to feature his rooftop forest in an upcoming documentary.

When the Covid-19 lockdown shut down travel in 2020, wildlife photographer Aman Sharma lost access to the forests and grasslands where he had been photographing birds since he was a teenager. Rather than wait out the confinement, he looked at the bare concrete terrace of his Delhi home and started planting.

Six years later, that terrace holds more than 500 native plants and has become one of Delhi's most closely watched private experiments in urban rewilding. "On this terrace, we have planted more than 500 plants. Because of that, we have seen more than 100 types of birds and more than 25 types of butterflies in Delhi," Sharma told Indicore in an interview reported by The Times of India.

Context and Background

Sharma's interest in birds started well before his teens. He began watching birds from his balcony as a schoolboy, and a bulbul building its nest nearby deepened his curiosity. That interest grew into wildlife photography and documentation, and eventually into Birds of India, an online platform that now reaches nearly 900,000 followers, according to The Better India.

The lockdown cut all of that off. "If I can't go to the birds, I'll make the birds come to me," he decided. With guidance from his grandmother, he began growing native trees, flowering plants, fruit-bearing species and vegetables chosen to provide food and shelter for local wildlife. The New Indian Express reported in 2020 on how he used indigenous plants and a mix of flowering and fruit-bearing species to draw in birds, bees and butterflies. Not everything survived. Plants died, some experiments failed, and he kept adapting.

Impact and Analysis

Sharma's central claim is that his approach differs from ordinary balcony gardening. Ornamental plants look good; his three categories each do a job.

First, host plants: species butterflies need to breed and complete their life cycle. Lemon is his example. Second, flowering plants — sadabahar, bougainvillea — that feed pollinators and add another layer to the canopy. Third, food-bearing plants for birds: chikoo, capsicum, pomegranate, brinjal and guava. Together they create overlapping resources rather than a single burst of flowers.

The result, he argues, is a system that keeps wildlife rather than merely attracting it for a visit. Insects colonize the plants; insects draw birds; the birds return to nest. Sunbirds, kingfishers and parakeets are among the visitors documented at the terrace. Speaking on Kaun Banega Crorepati, Sharma extended the idea: if thousands of ordinary homes planted even two or three host plants each, the network could function as a wildlife corridor for butterfly migration across a city. "If everyone's homes become like this, I think, for me, the world would change," he said.

"If you plant three types of plants, your home can also become an urban jungle."

— Aman Sharma, wildlife photographer and conservationist

Diaspora Angle

The story has already crossed oceans. After The Better India's social media team featured Sharma's journey, a filmmaker based in Los Angeles reached out to include his rooftop forest in an upcoming documentary — a project that began on a family terrace heading for audiences far beyond India. For readers far from Delhi, the replicability is the point: Sharma began with pots on a rooftop and insists a balcony, window or small terrace can start with a few carefully chosen plants.

What's Next

The documentary will take the terrace's message to a global audience, and the corridor idea Sharma floated on KBC remains the larger ambition — thousands of small plantings adding up to urban habitat. His own advice for starting is deliberately small: begin with one host plant, add a flowering plant, then a fruit- or food-bearing plant for birds. The terrace that began as a lockdown coping mechanism suggests urban wildlife does not always need a forest to begin with. Sometimes it begins with a few pots outside a window.
